network.overall_strategy: Represent ten distinct, literature-graded route variants rather than claim ten established syntheses of free cysteine. Three routes share experimentally supported N-acetylated serine-nitrile chemistry but use different sulfur-incorporation sequences. Their conversion to free cysteine requires explicitly speculative hydrolysis and deacetylation steps. Additional routes cover direct Strecker chemistry, serine/dehydroalanine chemistry, hydantoin chemistry, historical UV and discharge experiments, trace hydrothermal synthesis, and a kinetically disfavored computational proposal. The latter routes are not assigned the credibility or yields of the protected-nitrile chemistry. Glycolaldehyde, mercaptoacetaldehyde, thioacetic acid, and N-acetylimidazole are supplied small-molecule feedstocks; their environmental availability is not established by this graph. Experimental mixtures with unresolved mechanisms are represented by explicitly lumped reaction nodes, not invented elementary mechanisms. All conditions exclude molecular oxygen. Speculative temperature ranges are proposed assessment windows, not demonstrated productive conditions. Products have unspecified stereochemistry and no enantioenrichment is assumed. Neutral molecular representations stand for their condition-dependent protonation pools. Each environment_formed value records one representative setting; reaction nodes specify alternative formation environments. The intermediate role also covers coproducts because the requested schema has no coproduct category.

reactions.name: Glycolaldehyde Strecker synthesis of serine nitrile

conditions.other: Concentrated, anoxic aqueous feedstocks; mildly alkaline ammonia/cyanide solution; subsequent processing before extensive aminonitrile degradation.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia-carbonyl condensation and cyanide addition furnish the alpha-aminonitrile; water is the net condensation coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally supported precursor chemistry: Foden et al. (2020) identify glycolaldehyde Strecker chemistry as an effective source of serine nitrile. Patel et al. (2015) provide broader cyanosulfidic context for related feedstock production, not a completed cysteine synthesis. Natural concentration and coordinated delivery remain unresolved.

reactions.name: N,O-Acetylation of serine nitrile with an activated acetyl donor

conditions.other: Near-neutral to mildly alkaline solution; sufficient activated acetyl donor for both N- and O-acetylation; staged dosing may be needed to compete with donor hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitutions acetylate the amino and hydroxyl groups, releasing imidazole. The activated donor is a consumed reagent, not a catalyst.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report N-acetylimidazole as an alternative acetylating system. This avoids assuming a ferricyanide regeneration cycle in a reduced environment. The reported maximum 91% acetylation yield for the thioacetate/ferricyanide protocol is not assigned to this alternative. Environmental production and accumulation of N-acetylimidazole remain an explicit feedstock gap.

reactions.name: Acetate elimination to N-acetyldehydroalanine nitrile

conditions.other: Approximately pH 8; residence time of days; acetic acid is predominantly acetate at reaction pH.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile-assisted alpha-deprotonation and beta-elimination of acetate generate an N-acylated dehydroalanine nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) obtained approximately 85% N-acetyldehydroalanine nitrile after four days at pH 8 and room temperature. The nitrile facilitates elimination, while N-acylation suppresses rearrangement and subsequent aminothiol self-reaction. No cysteine-specific mineral catalyst is required.

reactions.name: Sulfide addition and nitrile thiohydration

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with sulfide-retaining aqueous confinement
conditions.other: Near-neutral solution with excess dissolved H2S/HS-; oxygen exclusion; avoid excessive dissolved iron that removes sulfide.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide adds to the activated alkene, and additional sulfide converts the nitrile functionality into a thioamide. This node summarizes the experimentally observed coupled transformations.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) observed near-quantitative conversion to an N-acetylcysteine thioamide. The product is a protected cysteinyl derivative, not free cysteine. Both its side-chain sulfur and thioamide sulfur require a sulfide supply; coefficients are implicit in the species-level graph.

reactions.name: Candidate hydrolysis of cysteine thioamide to N-acetylcysteine
agents: Hydronium ions for general acid catalysis

conditions.other: Acidic aqueous compartment, approximately pH 1-3; staged residence and rapid cooling; preservation of the side-chain thiol and N-acetyl group must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Net thioamide hydrolysis replaces the terminal sulfur/nitrogen functionality with a carboxyl group, releasing ammonia and hydrogen sulfide, potentially through amide or thioacid intermediates.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative free-cysteine closure step. Foden et al. (2020) establish the thioamide and related cysteinyl chemistry but do not establish this selective environmental conversion to an accumulating N-acetylcysteine pool. Hydrolysis is chemically possible, yet competing deacetylation, decomposition, and metal binding could prevent useful recovery.

reactions.name: Candidate N-deacetylation releasing free cysteine

conditions.other: Acidic, anoxic water; potentially long residence; prompt export into cooler conditions after hydrolysis; no enzymatic deacetylase is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the N-acetyl amide releases cysteine and acetic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative bottleneck required because the target is free cysteine rather than a protected cysteinyl residue. Foden et al. (2020) do not demonstrate an integrated, high-yield prebiotic deprotection sequence. Ordinary amide hydrolysis motivates this edge, but its rate relative to cysteine destruction must be established experimentally.

reactions.name: Thioacetate conjugate addition to protected dehydroalanine nitrile

conditions.other: Approximately pH 7; reaction time around 12 hours in the reported experiment; thioacetic acid is substantially ionized.

reactions.mechanism: Thioacetate undergoes conjugate addition to the activated double bond, installing the cysteine side chain as an S-acetyl thioester.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report essentially quantitative thioester formation in approximately 12 hours at pH 7. This experimentally supported alternative separates sulfur installation from subsequent thiol unmasking. Thioacetate availability remains a geochemical constraint.

reactions.name: Ammonolysis of the S-acetyl protecting group

conditions.other: Ammonia-rich, mildly alkaline solution; anoxic conditions; ammonia is a consumed acyl acceptor, not a mineral catalyst.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks the thioester carbonyl, releasing the side-chain thiol and producing acetamide while retaining N-acetyl protection.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) obtained N-acetylcysteine nitrile in approximately 77% yield by ammonolysis. Retaining N-acylation avoids the particularly unstable unprotected cysteine-nitrile state. The required ammonia activity and selectivity in mixed natural solutions remain environmental questions.

reactions.name: Candidate hydrolysis of N-acetylcysteine nitrile

conditions.other: Approximately pH 1-3; water in excess; staged acidification after ammonolysis; competing N-deacetylation must be quantified.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration and subsequent amide hydrolysis give the carboxylic acid and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative environmental closure based on standard nitrile chemistry, not a demonstrated high-yield continuation of Foden et al. (2020). The central uncertainty is whether nitrile hydrolysis can preserve the thiol and enough N-acetyl protection to avoid destructive side reactions.

reactions.name: Sulfide-mediated thiolysis and thioamide formation

conditions.other: Near-neutral aqueous sulfide in excess; strictly anoxic; sulfur incorporation and thioester exchange occur in the same reaction module.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide cleaves the S-acetyl thioester, regenerating thioacetic acid, while sulfide addition to the nitrile furnishes the cysteine thioamide.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report approximately 95% yield of the cysteine thioamide through thiolysis. This is distinct from both direct sulfide capture and ammonia-mediated S-deacetylation, although it converges on the same protected thioamide.

reactions.name: Candidate hydrolysis of serine nitrile to serine

conditions.other: Acidic geothermal pool, approximately pH 1-3; prolonged residence; solution must subsequently change conditions before sulfide addition.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the aminonitrile through an amide intermediate produces serine and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Standard Strecker completion is chemically justified, but this particular environmental implementation is not established by the supplied studies and is therefore speculative. Foden et al. (2020) support serine-nitrile availability; Parker et al. (2011) discuss serine as a candidate precursor without closing this complete sequence.

reactions.name: Hypothesized dehydration of unprotected serine

conditions.other: Warm wet-dry cycling; water removal alone is not established to provide sufficient activation; no effective abiotic catalyst is asserted.

reactions.mechanism: Formal alpha,beta-dehydration generates dehydroalanine, provided an otherwise unresolved activation process makes hydroxyl elimination competitive.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, likely inefficient bottleneck. Parker et al. (2011) proposed serine/dehydroalanine sulfurization, whereas Foden et al. (2020) emphasize the poor elimination chemistry and instability of unprotected intermediates. This edge must not be interpreted as demonstrated spontaneous dehydration at the stated temperature.

reactions.name: Hypothesized sulfide trapping of free dehydroalanine

conditions.other: Approximately pH 7-9; immediate sulfide delivery after formation of the transient electrophile; minimize residence without sulfide.

reactions.mechanism: Conjugate sulfide addition followed by proton transfer formally generates the cysteine skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Mechanistically proposed by Parker et al. (2011), not demonstrated as a complete prebiotic free-serine route. Unprotected dehydroalanine can rearrange, hydrolyze, or undergo other reactions before sulfide capture; the successful N-acyl nitrile chemistry of Foden et al. (2020) does not validate this unprotected analogue.

reactions.name: Low-yield direct mercaptoacetaldehyde Strecker branch

conditions.other: Approximately pH 9.2; minutes-to-hours observation window; aldehyde monomer represents its hydrated/dimer-equilibrating pool.

reactions.mechanism: Competing carbonyl, imine, and cyanohydrin equilibria permit only a minor aminonitrile branch; this is not direct displacement of cyanohydrin hydroxyl by ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Directly tested and strongly disfavored by Foden et al. (2020): cysteine nitrile remained below 5%, while a sulfur-containing cyanohydrin reached approximately 77% transiently and extensive degradation followed. Shalayel et al. (2018) discuss the precursor concept. The target-directed edge represents a minor product, not an efficient synthesis.

reactions.name: Hypothetical rescue hydrolysis of unstable cysteine nitrile
agents: Hydronium ions for nitrile hydrolysis and amino-group protonation

conditions.other: Immediate acidification to approximately pH 1-3 after the Strecker stage; rapid transfer is essential but not experimentally validated.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-promoted nitrile hydrolysis would produce cysteine if it outcompetes aminothiol-nitrile condensation and thermal destruction.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative rescue step with adverse experimental evidence. Foden et al. (2020) demonstrate cysteine-nitrile instability, not successful trapping by this procedure. Amino-group protonation provides a chemical reason to investigate acidification, but no useful overall yield or natural transport sequence is established.

reactions.name: Candidate carbon dioxide capture and serine-hydantoin formation

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with sustained dissolved inorganic carbon
conditions.other: Ammonia/carbonate-containing pool, approximately pH 8-10; dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and carbonate constitute one inorganic-carbon reservoir.

reactions.mechanism: Bucherer-Bergs-type carbamylation, cyclization, and rearrangement of an aminonitrile formally incorporate carbon dioxide into a hydantoin ring.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative route-specific implementation of established hydantoin-forming reaction chemistry. Parker et al. (2011) propose a serine-hydantoin branch, but the supplied evidence does not demonstrate this exact conversion and subsequent sulfurization in a realistic prebiotic mixture.

reactions.name: Hypothesized dehydration to a methylenehydantoin

conditions.other: Concentrating wet-dry cycles; an effective leaving-group activation mechanism remains unidentified.

reactions.mechanism: Formal elimination between the hydantoin ring carbon and hydroxymethyl substituent generates an exocyclic activated double bond.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative bottleneck in the hydantoin proposal of Parker et al. (2011). Ring carbonyls can stabilize the resulting conjugated system, but that does not establish an adequate dehydration rate or selectivity at the stated temperatures.

reactions.name: Candidate sulfide addition to methylenehydantoin

conditions.other: Near-neutral to mildly alkaline sulfide-containing water; rehydration after the proposed dehydration stage.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide adds to the exocyclic electron-poor alkene, installing a sulfanylmethyl substituent on the hydantoin ring.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically motivated but speculative within the supplied evidence. Parker et al. (2011) propose the hydantoin analogue of dehydroalanine sulfurization; neither productive precursor accumulation nor a complete prebiotic sequence was demonstrated.

reactions.name: Candidate hydrolytic opening of cysteine hydantoin
agents: Alkaline aqueous medium for base-promoted ring hydrolysis

conditions.other: Approximately pH 10-12; long residence may be necessary; products are represented after protonation-state normalization; cool promptly after ring opening.

reactions.mechanism: Hydantoin ring opening and subsequent carbamoyl-group hydrolysis release the amino acid, ammonia, and inorganic carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative environmental completion of the hydantoin proposal in Parker et al. (2011). Hydantoin hydrolysis is chemically established in general, but sufficient conversion under natural alkalinity while preserving cysteine is not demonstrated here. Hydrothermal heating may accelerate both release and destruction.

reactions.name: Lumped H2S-sensitized atmospheric UV branch

conditions.other: Anoxic, locally reducing volcanic gas/aerosol setting; UV wavelengths overlapping H2S absorption and plausible surface transmission; aqueous collection of products.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved photochemical network initiated by H2S photolysis and energetic hydrogen chemistry, followed by carbon-nitrogen-sulfur assembly and condensate reactions. Hydrogen is a representative net redox coproduct, not a measured cysteine-specific yield.
reactions.reasoning: Sagan and Khare (1971) and Hong et al. (1974) report sulfur-containing amino-acid chemistry with overall amino-acid quantum yields around 10^-5. Some historical identifications concern cystine or cysteine/cystine-class products, so the free-cysteine output is provisional. This node neither requires oxygen-mediated cystine formation nor establishes a resolved anoxic molecular mechanism; modern analytical replication is needed.

reactions.name: Lumped reducing-gas electrical-discharge branch

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk collection region; discharge is nonthermal
conditions.other: Lightning or electrical discharge through locally reducing, H2S-containing gas; water vapor and condensate cycling; no globally methane-rich atmosphere is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved discharge-driven radical and carbonyl/cyanide chemistry produces a complex mixture subsequently processed in condensate. The node is a coarse-grained candidate cysteine-producing branch, not an elementary reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Parker et al. (2011) summarize historical sulfur-amino-acid discharge reports and reanalyze Miller's H2S experiment. Their archived samples contained no surviving cysteine; cysteamine and other compounds only support an indirect inference of earlier cysteine-related chemistry. Consequently, this free-cysteine branch has lower evidential certainty than the modern protected-nitrile reactions.

reactions.name: Lumped mineral-buffered hydrothermal trace-cysteine synthesis
agents: Pyrite as part of the experimental redox-buffering assemblage
Pyrrhotite as part of the experimental redox-buffering assemblage
Magnetite as part of the experimental redox-buffering assemblage
Trace platinum present in the experimental apparatus; no cysteine-specific catalytic role established

conditions.other: Experimental reference mixture: approximately 0.19 M cyanide, 0.23 M ammonium chloride, 0.18 M formaldehyde, and 0.05 M sulfide under CO2/H2; these concentrations are not asserted to represent natural fluids.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved multistep carbonyl/cyanide/ammonium/sulfide chemistry under mineral-buffered conditions. Ammonia appears on both sides to represent nitrogen transfer and regeneration in a possible aminonitrile-based net description, not established isotope mapping.
reactions.reasoning: Hennet, Holm and Engel (1992) reported cysteine only at trace/present levels, despite concentrated reagents. The minerals were associated with the experimental redox environment, not demonstrated cysteine-specific catalysts. This node preserves the empirical observation without assigning an unsupported detailed mechanism or assuming universal sulfide abundance in alkaline vents.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde Strecker synthesis of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Concentrated formaldehyde, ammonia, and cyanide; mildly alkaline solution; subsequent hydrolysis is a separate stage.

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation from formaldehyde and ammonia followed by cyanide addition yields the glycine aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Standard Strecker chemistry provides a chemically justified glycine precursor module. Foden et al. (2020) discuss the same aminonitrile-forming reaction class, and Hennet et al. (1992) obtained abundant glycine from related feedstocks. Assignment of this isolated intermediate to a particular natural reactor remains an inference, not a demonstrated cysteine pathway.

reactions.name: Candidate aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis to glycine

conditions.other: Acidic geothermal water; prolonged hydrolysis followed by transfer into the separately supplied sulfur-carbonyl reaction zone.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis yield glycine and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Standard chemical transformation with a speculative environmental implementation. Slavova et al. (2025) experimentally obtained glycine from different formamide/water feedstocks, not by validating this exact module. This alternative glycine supply avoids treating their computational upstream network as experimentally closed.

reactions.name: Proposed formaldehyde-hydrogen sulfide thiohemiacetal formation

conditions.pressure: 10-30 bar to maintain an aqueous phase
conditions.other: Dissolved formaldehyde and reduced sulfur; water mediates proton transfer; this pressure range is an assessment setting, not the reported formamide experiment.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen sulfide addition to the carbonyl, assisted by solvent proton transfer, gives hydroxymethanethiol.
reactions.reasoning: Computationally supported, not an experimentally established cysteine-producing step. Slavova et al. (2025) calculate a water-mediated barrier around 26.4 kcal/mol for this precursor chemistry. Reversibility and competition with other formaldehyde reactions constrain accumulation.

reactions.name: Proposed dehydration to transient thioformaldehyde

conditions.other: Transient local production only; rapid hydration, oligomerization, and sulfur exchange compete with subsequent capture.

reactions.mechanism: Formal loss of water from the thiohemiacetal generates the thiocarbonyl compound.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative precursor edge in the computational network of Slavova et al. (2025). Bulk aqueous conditions do not by themselves favor accumulation of monomeric thioformaldehyde. This species is treated as transient, not as a stable hydrothermal reservoir.

reactions.name: Kinetically disfavored proposed glycine-thioformaldehyde coupling

conditions.temperature: 413-433 K assessment window; productive cysteine formation is not established
conditions.other: No demonstrated catalyst lowers the decisive barrier; inclusion records a computational hypothesis, not a practical synthesis recommendation.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed alpha-carbon coupling of glycine with thioformaldehyde, accompanied by proton transfers, forms the cysteine carbon skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Computational-only and strongly kinetically disfavored. Slavova et al. (2025) calculate a barrier of approximately 55.9 kcal/mol despite an exothermic product, and their experiments did not produce cysteine. Exothermicity does not establish an appreciable rate; this branch is retained as an explicitly unvalidated comparator rather than an effective source.

pathways.name: Protected serine nitrile via direct sulfide capture
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde supplies serine nitrile, acetylation enables elimination, and sulfide gives the experimentally supported cysteine thioamide. Hydrolysis and N-deacetylation are speculative requirements for reaching free cysteine. These stages require sequential environments rather than one-pot compatibility.

pathways.name: Protected serine nitrile via thioacetate and ammonolysis
pathways.description: Thioacetate installs protected sulfur, and ammonia selectively unmasks the thiol to furnish N-acetylcysteine nitrile. The sulfur-installation and ammonolysis modules are experimentally supported; selective nitrile hydrolysis and final deacetylation are unvalidated environmental closure steps.

pathways.name: Protected serine nitrile via thioacetate and sulfide thiolysis
pathways.description: Thioacetate addition is followed by sulfide-mediated thiolysis and nitrile-to-thioamide conversion, regenerating thioacetic acid. This experimentally supported sulfur-processing variant converges with P1 before the same speculative free-cysteine release steps.

pathways.name: Direct mercaptoacetaldehyde Strecker route with hypothetical rescue
pathways.description: A minor, experimentally observed cysteine-nitrile branch is followed by hypothetical rapid hydrolysis. This route is strongly disfavored because cysteine nitrile forms below 5% and readily degrades; neither precursor supply nor rescue hydrolysis is established as an effective natural process.

pathways.name: Unprotected serine-dehydroalanine sulfurization
pathways.description: Serine nitrile is hydrolyzed to serine, which would need effective dehydration followed by immediate sulfide trapping. This is a mechanistically motivated proposal, not a demonstrated end-to-end synthesis; dehydration and transient-intermediate survival are decisive bottlenecks.

pathways.name: Hydantoin-protected sulfurization
pathways.description: A proposed hydantoin branch incorporates inorganic carbon, generates an exocyclic alkene, adds sulfide, and releases cysteine by ring hydrolysis. The sequence implements the literature hypothesis but is not experimentally closed; dehydration and sufficiently mild hydantoin hydrolysis remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Historical H2S-driven UV synthesis
pathways.description: A lumped atmospheric-photochemical route from simple gases reflects historical sulfur-amino-acid reports. Individual intermediates remain unresolved, and identification of specifically free cysteine under continuously anoxic conditions is provisional. The overall amino-acid quantum yields are not cysteine-specific yields.

pathways.name: Historical H2S-containing electrical-discharge synthesis
pathways.description: A separate, lumped lightning/discharge route represents historical cysteine-related reports from reducing gas mixtures. Archived Miller samples did not retain detectable cysteine, so the free-cysteine branch is uncertain and is not reconstructed through invented intermediates.

pathways.name: Empirical mineral-buffered hydrothermal trace route
pathways.description: A lumped experimental route represents trace cysteine reported from concentrated formaldehyde, cyanide, ammonium, and sulfide under mineral-buffered hydrothermal conditions. It establishes a reported trace product, not a selective mechanism, demonstrated mineral catalysis, or environmentally realistic productivity.

pathways.name: Computational glycine-thioformaldehyde route
pathways.description: The sequence lists dependency-ordered precursor branches: glycine is prepared first, thioformaldehyde is supplied separately, and the streams converge at the proposed coupling. The calculated 55.9 kcal/mol barrier makes this an unvalidated, kinetically disfavored comparator, not an established productive pathway at the stated conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Foden et al. (2020) strongly support the protected serine-nitrile sequence through N-acetylcysteine thioamide. This evidence does not establish the subsequent production of free cysteine. Reactions rxn_005 and rxn_006 are chemically conceivable net hydrolyses, but productive conditions, selectivity and cysteine survival are unverified. Surface-to-hydrothermal transfer is not intrinsically inconsistent, but the submitted network provides neither a physical transfer model nor quantitative hydrolysis conditions. All reactions conserve atoms and charge with the supplied coefficients.
suggestions: Measure thioamide hydrolysis, N-deacetylation and competing decomposition under explicit anoxic temperature, pH and residence-time conditions.
Demonstrate free cysteine analytically rather than extrapolating from the yield of protected cysteinyl products.
Specify a transport and heating scenario that preserves the protected intermediate, and write the inferred stoichiometric coefficients explicitly.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Foden et al. (2020) support thioacetate addition and subsequent ammonolysis to N-acetylcysteine nitrile; the reported protected-nitrile yield must not be interpreted as a free-cysteine yield. Nitrile hydrolysis offers a conventional prospective connection to N-acetylcysteine, making this a narrowly preferred candidate for completing the stated target synthesis. Nevertheless, rxn_009 and rxn_006 remain unvalidated in the proposed environmental sequence, including whether nitrile hydrolysis can occur before premature deprotection or destructive side reactions.
suggestions: Establish a hydrolysis window that converts the nitrile while controlling N-acetyl cleavage and thiol-containing side products.
Test the complete sequence in carried-forward reaction mixtures, including residual ammonia, acetamide and acetylating reagents.
Provide reaction-level citations, concentrations and conditions, together with a physically justified transfer into the hydrolysis environment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The thioacetate-addition and sulfide-thiolysis sequence is well aligned with Foden et al. (2020), including strong experimental support for formation of the cysteine thioamide. Reaction rxn_010 is balanced using two equivalents of H2S and is not a conservation violation. This route then inherits the same unresolved thioamide-hydrolysis and N-deacetylation bottlenecks as P1. Its additional experimentally supported sulfur-processing sequence does not independently validate formation or preservation of free cysteine.
suggestions: Test rxn_005 and rxn_006 with the actual sulfide- and thioacetate-containing output of rxn_010.
Specify sulfide concentration and pH to distinguish conjugate addition, S-deacetylation and nitrile thiohydration.
Quantify free cysteine formation and destruction during hydrothermal exposure and subsequent recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The network correctly acknowledges the negative experimental evidence. Foden et al. (2020) observed less than 5% cysteine nitrile and extensive degradation during direct mercaptoacetaldehyde Strecker chemistry. Reaction rxn_015 is a formally reasonable nitrile hydrolysis, but no evidence shows that it outcompetes aminothiol-nitrile self-reaction or polymerization. Transfer and heating do not constitute a demonstrated rescue mechanism and could increase competing destruction. The pathway is balanced but lacks credible end-to-end kinetic closure.
suggestions: Measure cysteine-nitrile formation, decomposition and hydrolysis rates in the same reaction mixture.
Demonstrate a specific trapping, compartmentalization or rapid-transfer mechanism that preserves the transient nitrile.
Require direct free-cysteine identification before treating the proposed rescue as productive.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This follows the mechanistically informed serine/dehydroalanine proposal discussed by Parker et al. (2011), rather than an experimentally closed synthesis. Serine-nitrile hydrolysis is plausible under suitable conditions, but rxn_012 lacks demonstrated activation for eliminating the hydroxyl group of unprotected serine. Free dehydroalanine is also unstable, so sulfide addition in rxn_013 must compete with tautomerization, hydrolysis and other diversion reactions. A Surface label alone does not establish a productive dehydration-and-trapping regime.
suggestions: Identify and demonstrate an activation mechanism for serine dehydration under the stated environmental conditions.
Measure dehydroalanine lifetime and sulfide-trapping selectivity rather than assuming quantitative passage through this intermediate.
Specify separate conditions for nitrile hydrolysis and dehydration, including how the reaction mixture transitions between them.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin strategy has recognizable chemical precedent and matches the proposal discussed by Parker et al. (2011), but the supplied research does not demonstrate this complete sequence. Aminonitrile-to-hydantoin conversion requires suitable carbon dioxide/carbonate chemistry and cyclization conditions, not merely coexistence of the listed molecules. Dehydration in rxn_017 is the principal activation uncertainty. Sulfide addition to a methylenehydantoin is plausible, while ring opening in rxn_019 requires conditions that release cysteine without excessive destruction.
suggestions: Specify carbon dioxide activity, carbonate/ammonium speciation, pH and reaction time for serine-hydantoin formation.
Experimentally establish methylenehydantoin formation and its selectivity toward sulfide addition.
Demonstrate hydantoin hydrolysis and quantify cysteine recovery under anoxic conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: An empirical lumped node is appropriate for the unresolved H2S-sensitized photochemical mixtures studied by Sagan and Khare (1971) and Hong et al. (1974). Historical reports support cysteine/cystine-class products, but cystine detection is not equivalent to demonstrated accumulation of free cysteine under the network's anoxic conditions. The balanced equation is acceptable bookkeeping, not evidence that H2 is the sole coproduct or that the target forms selectively. A surface or plume setting is plausible, but wavelength, photon flux, gas composition and product collection are unspecified.
suggestions: Attach the specific experimental citation and distinguish cysteine from cystine and any workup-dependent products.
Specify the irradiation spectrum, photon flux, gas partial pressures and gas-liquid collection geometry.
Replicate target identification with modern quantitative analysis and labeled feedstocks; report cysteine-specific yield rather than total amino-acid quantum yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Historical discharge reports provide some support for cysteine or cystine formation in reducing sulfur-containing mixtures. However, Parker et al. (2011) found no surviving cysteine in the archived Miller samples; associated degradation products are suggestive rather than direct confirmation. The lumped representation is appropriate, but the particular gas mixture and free-cysteine endpoint need a clearly matched experimental source. Locally reducing volcanic-plume discharge is physically plausible without assuming a globally reducing atmosphere.
suggestions: Identify which historical experiment supports this exact feedstock mixture and whether cysteine was measured directly.
Specify gas partial pressures, discharge energy, aqueous collection conditions and residence times.
Measure formation and destruction simultaneously, distinguishing free cysteine, cystine and cysteamine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hennet, Holm and Engel (1992) provide direct empirical support for reported trace cysteine in a mineral-buffered hydrothermal mixture. Trace production can satisfy target formation; low yield alone does not invalidate this branch. Confidence is limited by the trace-level evidence and the absence of the experimental concentrations, mineral assemblage, gas phase and operating conditions from the submitted reaction record. Ammonia appearing on both sides is balance-compatible, but the net equation does not determine nitrogen provenance or mechanism.
suggestions: Specify the approximately 150 degrees C, 10 atm experimental conditions, concentrated reagent solutions and CO2/H2 gas phase when invoking this precedent.
Document pyrite, pyrrhotite and magnetite as the redox-buffering assemblage, including potential contributions from the TiO2 liner and trace Pt.
Confirm trace cysteine with modern analytical controls and determine whether it persists under the actual mineral-buffered conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The glycine and sulfur-containing C1 precursor branches are structurally coherent, but the final coupling is not a credible productive step without additional evidence. Slavova et al. (2025) calculated an approximately 55.9 kcal/mol barrier for the cysteine-forming coupling and did not experimentally detect cysteine in their precursor experiments. Exothermic product formation does not remove that kinetic obstacle. Thioformaldehyde generation and persistence in hot aqueous mixtures also remain unresolved. The empirical trace result represented by rxn_022 does not validate this particular mechanism.
suggestions: Retain this as a computational hypothesis unless an experimentally supported lower-barrier coupling mechanism is identified.
Measure thioformaldehyde formation, hydration and oligomerization under explicit hydrothermal conditions.
Use labeled glycine and sulfur-containing C1 precursors to test cysteine formation while independently measuring substrate and product decomposition.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally strong: its 34 molecule nodes and 27 reaction nodes form a connected graph, molecule IDs are consistent, and the deterministic check establishes zero atom/charge conservation violations. The 12 coefficient-dependent reactions require modest coefficients that should be recorded explicitly; they are not unbalanced reactions. Supplied feedstocks are accepted as boundary inputs, not treated as missing synthesis steps. Literature alignment is good at the strategy level because the network distinguishes protected-product demonstrations, historical reports, trace synthesis, failed direct Strecker chemistry and computational proposals. However, the submitted reaction records contain no reaction-level citations or quantitative temperature, pressure, pH, concentration and residence-time specifications, despite references to proposed conditions in the strategy. P1-P3 convincingly reach protected cysteinyl intermediates but do not establish their conversion to surviving free cysteine. P9 provides the clearest direct, although trace-level, target evidence, while P2 is the strongest prospective multistep completion. The empirical lumped nodes are legitimate representations of unresolved mixtures, but their balanced equations do not establish exclusive products or mechanisms. Environmental confidence is limited by unspecified delivery, transfer, mineral/redox conditions and formation-versus-destruction kinetics, not by the number or order of environments. Problematic reactions are flagged for these evidential or chemical limitations, not conservation failures. Overall confidence reflects end-to-end target production rather than route count or shared intermediates. The network is not approved at the required 0.90 threshold.
